# Introduction and Description

## Learning Benchmarking Tool

Business Monitor developed the Learning Benchmarking Tool (LBT) to support organisations in evaluating and comparing the effectiveness of their learning programmes [@BusinessMonitor2026, p. 4]. The tool applies the Kirkpatrick framework to measure learning effectiveness across four levels: Reaction (L1), Learning (L2), Behaviour (L3), and Results (L4) [@BusinessMonitor2026, pp. 4, 11-12].

The original LBT was developed as a proof of concept using a fully synthetic organisational dataset [@BusinessMonitor2026, p. 4]. Its data structures include both programme-level and participant-level data and were designed to be compatible with future real organisational data [@BusinessMonitor2026, p. 10]. The current MVP therefore demonstrates the analytical logic without processing real participant data. The original project identifies piloting with real organisational data as a next step towards an operational benchmarking service [@BusinessMonitor2026, pp. 27-29].

For the purpose of this data protection assessment, an operational scenario is considered in which Business Monitor administers participant surveys on behalf of participating organisations.[^1] Business Monitor therefore initially processes the participant information required to invite participants and administer the surveys. After collection, participant-level survey and learning data are pseudonymised for analytical processing.

[^1]: This is an operational assumption adopted for the present data protection assessment. The original LBT report assumes that participating organisations submit aggregated or pseudonymised data and does not specify that Business Monitor itself administers participant surveys; see @BusinessMonitor2026, p. 29.

These data are subsequently used to calculate programme-level indicators across the four Kirkpatrick levels. The original MVP already aggregates programme- and participant-level data into comparable KPIs and benchmarking outputs [@BusinessMonitor2026, pp. 11-13]. For the operational scenario assessed in this report, the analytical functionality is extended to programme-level predictive models intended to predict learning outcomes and KPIs rather than the performance, behaviour, or capabilities of individual participants.[^2]

[^2]: This programme-level predictive functionality is an assumption for the intended operational LBT. In the original MVP, the Random Forest and Gradient Boosting models are described as explanatory rather than predictive and are used to identify the importance of design and contextual variables in explaining KPI variation; see @BusinessMonitor2026, p. 12.

The resulting programme-level data can contribute to cross-organisational benchmarking. This is consistent with the LBT value proposition, in which Business Monitor acts as a neutral hub that aggregates learning evaluation data to enable comparisons across participating organisations [@BusinessMonitor2026, pp. 6-7]. Benchmark results presented to customers are intended to be aggregated and anonymised.

## Personal Data and Data Subjects

For this assessment, the processing can be considered in three data layers. First, survey administration involves directly identifiable personal data, such as participant contact details required to administer the survey. Second, the analytical layer contains pseudonymised participant-level data, including survey responses, learning measurements, and contextual information relevant to the calculation of the programme-level indicators. The original LBT data model already distinguishes between programme-level and participant-level data and includes participant responses, behavioural indicators, and contextual information [@BusinessMonitor2026, pp. 10, 32-33].

Article 4(5) GDPR defines pseudonymisation as processing personal data in such a manner that the data can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information, provided that such additional information is kept separately and subject to appropriate technical and organisational measures [@GDPR, art. 4(5)]. Pseudonymisation does not in itself remove these data from the scope of the GDPR. Recital 26 states that pseudonymised personal data that could be attributed to a natural person through the use of additional information should be considered information relating to an identifiable natural person [@GDPR, recital 26].

Third, programme-level indicators and cross-organisational benchmark results are aggregated, with the intention that the final benchmark outputs no longer permit individual participants to be identified. This follows the intended deployment direction described in the original LBT report, in which outputs should be reported at a level where re-identification is not reasonably possible [@BusinessMonitor2026, p. 29]. The principal data subjects in the operational scenario are the employees or other individuals participating in the learning programmes.

The standard LBT is not designed to collect special categories of personal data within the meaning of Article 9 GDPR [@GDPR, art. 9(1)]. Nevertheless, the survey process may create a risk that such information is provided unintentionally, for example through free-text responses. Whether such fields are necessary and how this risk can be minimised therefore requires consideration when applying the data protection principles.

## GDPR Actors

The allocation of GDPR roles depends on the particular processing operation. Article 4(7) GDPR defines a controller as the natural or legal person or other body that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. Article 4(8) defines a processor as an entity that processes personal data on behalf of the controller [@GDPR, art. 4(7)-(8)].

In the operational LBT scenario, a participating organisation determines why the learning effectiveness of its employees is evaluated and may therefore qualify as controller for that processing purpose. Business Monitor may act as processor where it administers surveys and performs agreed analytical activities on the organisation's behalf.

Business Monitor's role may, however, differ when data from multiple participating organisations are subsequently used for the cross-organisational benchmarking service. The original business model positions Business Monitor as a neutral hub for cross-organisational data collaboration and benchmarking [@BusinessMonitor2026, pp. 6-7]. If Business Monitor independently determines the purpose and essential means of this subsequent processing, it may qualify as controller for that separate processing activity. The relevant GDPR roles must therefore be assessed per processing operation rather than assigning Business Monitor a single role for the LBT as a whole.

The following sections assess these processing activities against the GDPR data protection principles, examine the applicable lawful bases, and develop recommendations for the compliant operation of the LBT.

# How Are the Data Processed?

## Purpose of the processing

The LBT involves five processing operations, each with its own purpose: survey administration; participant-level learning analysis; programme-level calculation of the Kirkpatrick L1 to L4 indicators; programme-level predictive analytics; and cross-organisational benchmarking.[^3] Under the working hypothesis of Section 1, the first four serve the participating organisation's evaluation of its own programmes, with Business Monitor acting on its behalf. Benchmarking serves a different aim: Business Monitor's service to multiple organisations.

[^3]: Operations two and three are closely linked and may be merged after review. They are kept separate here because only the former processes personal data at participant level.

## Application of the data protection principles

### Lawfulness, fairness and transparency

Lawfulness is assessed in Section 3. Fairness and transparency are tested here, because the employment relationship leaves participants little real choice about taking part.[^4] Processing is unfair if participants cannot foresee that their answers also feed a commercial benchmark. If Business Monitor obtains contact details from the employer rather than from the participant, it must inform participants at the latest at the first contact, the survey invitation;[^5] information on the answers collected from participants themselves falls under Article 13.[^6] The information must be concise, intelligible and in plain language,[^7] name each controller and state each purpose, including benchmarking.[^8] A further purpose must be notified before that processing starts.[^9] Without such notice, the reasonable expectations on which the Article 6(4) assessment below depends cannot be met.

[^4]: @GDPR, art. 5(1)(a) and recital 39.

[^5]: @GDPR, art. 14(1) and (3)(b).

[^6]: @GDPR, art. 13(1).

[^7]: @GDPR, art. 12(1).

[^8]: @GDPR, art. 13(1)(a) and (c), art. 14(1)(a) and (c).

[^9]: @GDPR, art. 13(3).

### Purpose limitation

Article 5(1)(b) GDPR requires specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and prohibits further processing that is incompatible with them.[^10] Benchmarking is the critical transition: participants provide data for their employer's evaluation, and the data later feed a product used by other organisations.

[^10]: @GDPR, art. 5(1)(b).

Compatibility depends on the factors in Article 6(4).[^11] The link is strong, since benchmarking uses the same indicators for the same evaluative aim. The context is weaker: employees expect their employer to evaluate a programme, not that their answers inform a commercial comparison between companies, and the employment relationship limits their real choice.

[^11]: @GDPR, art. 6(4).

Article 5(1)(b) offers a second route: further processing for statistical purposes is not considered incompatible, in accordance with Article 89(1). Under Recital 162 the result must be aggregate data not used in support of decisions regarding a particular natural person,[^12] which fits the programme-level design of the LBT. This route supports the Article 6(4) assessment but does not replace it. Benchmarking is therefore compatible only if participants are told in advance, outputs are demonstrably aggregate, and no output is used for decisions about individuals.

[^12]: @GDPR, art. 5(1)(b), art. 89(1) and recital 162.

### Data minimisation

Article 5(1)(c) limits data to what is necessary for each purpose.[^13] Directly identifying data are needed only for survey administration; analysis needs the pseudonymous identifier and the measured variables. The original data model also holds participant-level variables such as location, a manager-support rating and a promotion flag.[^14] Each must be shown to be necessary; the promotion flag in particular records an employment outcome, whereas the indicator needs only a programme-level count. Free-text fields should be avoided, as they invite unnecessary or special-category data.

[^13]: @GDPR, art. 5(1)(c).

[^14]: @BusinessMonitor2026, p. 33.

### Accuracy

Article 5(1)(d) requires data to be accurate and, where necessary, up to date.[^15] Most LBT indicators rest on self-reported Likert scores, which the original report itself describes as subject to response bias,[^16] and follow-up measurements link responses over time through the pseudonymous identifier.

[^15]: @GDPR, art. 5(1)(d).

[^16]: @BusinessMonitor2026, p. 18.

### Storage limitation

Article 5(1)(e) allows identifiable data to be kept only as long as necessary.[^17] The three data layers need different periods. Identification data and the mapping are necessary only until the last follow-up measurement of the survey cycle and must then be deleted, as the case definition provides. Deleting the mapping can make the analytical data anonymous, but only if neither Business Monitor nor any other person could still identify participants by means reasonably likely to be used.[^18] That is doubtful where the participating organisation knows who attended a programme, and in small cohorts, such as the original design's minimum of eight participants, where combinations of contextual variables can single people out.[^19] Only aggregated outputs with a sufficient minimum cohort size can reliably fall outside the GDPR.

[^17]: @GDPR, art. 5(1)(e).

[^18]: @GDPR, recital 26.

[^19]: @BusinessMonitor2026, pp. 13-14.

### Integrity and confidentiality

Article 5(1)(f) requires appropriate security.[^20] Business Monitor would hold identifiable contact data and the key that reverses pseudonymisation. Stored next to the analytical data, that key would make pseudonymisation largely pointless, because Article 4(5) requires additional information to be kept separately and protected. Access should be limited to the staff who administer the survey.

[^20]: @GDPR, art. 5(1)(f) and art. 32(1).

### Accountability

Article 5(2) makes the controller responsible for demonstrating compliance:[^21] the participating organisation, and Business Monitor for benchmarking if it is controller there. The agreements and records proposed in Section 4 should allocate these responsibilities.

[^21]: @GDPR, art. 5(2).

# On Which Legal Basis?

## The processing ground relied on

As already noted in previous sections, there are two distinct processing purposes in the operational LBT scenario. The first purpose is the participating organisation's evaluation of its own learning programmes, for which Business Monitor acts as a processor. The second purpose is Business Monitor's cross-organisational benchmarking service, which may involve Business Monitor acting as a controller. For both purposes, the processing ground relied on is legitimate interests under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR [^22]. This ground is appropriate because the processing is necessary for the legitimate interests of both the participating organisation and Business Monitor, and these interests are not overridden by the rights and freedoms of the data subjects, as required by the balancing test in Article 6(1)(f) and recital 47.[^22]

The intent is for no special categories of personal data to be collected. As such, Article 9 of the GDPR should not apply. However, as previously noted, there is a risk that special categories of data may be inadvertently collected through free-text responses. In such cases, an Article 9 ground would be required, and the only applicable ground in this context would be explicit consent [^23] from the data subjects. This however may prove to be an issue, which will be further discussed in Section 3.3. Therefore, it is essential to minimize the collection of special categories of data and implement measures to prevent their inadvertent collection.

[^22]: @GDPR, art. 6(1)(f) and recital 47.
[^23]: @GDPR, art. 9(1) and art. 9(2)(a).

## Application of its criteria

### Organizational evaluation

For this use case, the legitimate interest is for the participating organisation to evaluate the effectiveness of its employee training/learning programmes, which is a credible interest in the context of organisational development and human resource management.
The processing of the relevant data is necessary to achieve this purpose; contact details are required to administer the survey to participants, and the (pseudonymised) survey responses and learning measurements are necessary to calculate and assess the effectiveness of the learning programmes. It may be possible to achieve the same purpose with less data, for example by using aggregated data or true anonymisation. Whether this impacts the ability to evaluate the effectiveness of the learning programmes depends on the nature of the program itself and the intended evaluation of the participating organisation.
In general, it would be reasonable for participating employees to expect their employer to evaluate the learning programme(s) they participated in, though given the employment relationship, they may have limited choice in whether or not to participate. Therefore, it is important for the participating organisation to provide clear and transparent information to participants about the purpose of the data processing, the types of data collected, and how their data will be used in the evaluation process. This can help ensure that participants are aware of their rights and can make informed decisions about their participation. The pseudonymisation of the data already helps mitigate some of the impact on participants, though pseudonymisation does not make the data unidentifiable and therefore does not remove the need for appropriate safeguards and transparency.

### Business Monitor's benchmarking service

For the second use case, the legitimate interest is for Business Monitor to provide a benchmarking service to multiple organisations, which is a credible (albeit arguably weaker) legitimate interest in the context of providing a commercial service.
The processing of data from multiple organisations' learning programmes is necessary to achieve this purpose, as it allows for the aggregation and comparison of data to generate meaningful benchmarks. The intent is for the benchmarking outputs to be aggregated, which helps mitigate the impact on participants. However, there is still a risk of re-identification, particularly in small cohorts, when contextual variables are included in the analysis, or when the participating organisations hold information that could be used to identify individuals. True anonymisation should be considered as it would further mitigate this risk, though it would have to be balanced against its impact on the ability to generate meaningful benchmarks. Both Business Monitor and the participating organisations should be transparent about the purpose of the benchmarking service, the types of data collected, and how the data will be used in the benchmarking process. Additionally, Business Monitor should implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to prevent re-identification and ensure that the rights and freedoms of participants are respected.
While employees may reasonably expect their employer to evaluate the learning programme(s) they participated in, it would not be reasonable for them to expect that their data would additionally be used for a commercial benchmarking service. Therefore, it is important for Business Monitor to provide a clear notice in advance to participants about the benchmarking purpose, the data collected, the measures in place (including pseudonymisation, aggregation, potential anonymisation, and any other technical and organisational safeguards), and how their data will be used in the benchmarking process. This can help ensure that participants are aware of their rights and can make informed decisions about their participation.

## Problems with relying on this ground

In general, while legitimate interests can provide a lawful basis for processing, it tends to be more difficult to justify compared to other grounds. A proper balancing test must be conducted to ensure that the legitimate interests of the controller do not override the rights and freedoms of the data subjects. This requires careful consideration of the potential risks and impacts on participants, as well as the implementation of appropriate safeguards to protect their personal data. Even then, the reliance on legitimate interests may be challenged if participants feel that their rights have been infringed upon or if they were not adequately informed about the processing activities. Therefore, it is essential for both the participating organisations and Business Monitor to maintain transparency, provide clear information, and implement robust data protection measures to ensure compliance with GDPR requirements.
Most other grounds laid out in Article 6(1) [^24] do not apply to either processing purpose. This includes compliance with a legal obligation, protecting vital interests, and public interest or official authority. Contractual necessity does not apply either, as the processing of data for the purposes of learning programme evaluation and benchmarking is not strictly necessary for the performance of a contract between the employee and employer. Consent could be considered, but it is not a reliable ground in the context of an employment relationship, where there may be a power imbalance and employees may feel pressured to consent. Therefore, legitimate interests remains the most appropriate ground for processing in this scenario, again provided that the necessary safeguards and transparency measures are implemented to protect the rights and freedoms of the data subjects.
As mentioned in Section 3.1, the processing of special categories of personal data under Article 9 of the GDPR would require explicit consent from the data subjects, as none of the other grounds in Article 9(2) apply. However, the same problems with article 6's consent ground apply to article 9's explicit consent ground [^23]. As such, it would be best to avoid the collection of special categories of personal data altogether, and to implement measures to prevent their inadvertent collection, such as avoiding free-text fields in surveys and providing clear instructions to participants about the types of information that should not be included in their responses.

[^24]: @GDPR, art. 6(1).

# Advice

## Alternatives to personal data

*Person A. Anonymisation, pseudonymisation, or using non-personal data instead.*

## Technical and organisational measures

The risks identified in Section 2 lead to five measures.

*Specify the benchmarking purpose.* The invitation should state the benchmarking purpose separately, as set out in Section 2.2.1.

*Tie retention to purpose.* A written schedule should set a period for each data layer. Identification data and the mapping are deleted after the last follow-up wave and the deletion is logged; analytical data have a defined maximum period and periodic review.

*Separate and protect identity data.* Identity data and the mapping are stored apart from the analytical dataset, encrypted, with the key held separately and access restricted by role and logged.[^25]

[^25]: @GDPR, art. 32(1)(a)-(b).

*Prevent re-identification.* A minimum cohort size applies to every benchmark output, small groups are suppressed, and the eight-participant threshold of the original design is tested for sufficiency.[^26]

[^26]: @BusinessMonitor2026, pp. 13-14.

*Document the processing.* Data protection by design and by default,[^27] a processor agreement between each organisation and Business Monitor,[^28] records of processing,[^29] and a documented DPIA screening before operation,[^30] because employee data from several organisations are combined.

[^27]: @GDPR, art. 25(1)-(2).

[^28]: @GDPR, art. 28(3).

[^29]: @GDPR, art. 30.

[^30]: @GDPR, art. 35.
